analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one House Republican with no cosponsors, was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have erased three taxes on passing wealth from one person to another: the estate tax charged on very large estates when someone dies, the gift tax charged on large transfers while living, and a tax aimed at skipping a generation to avoid estate taxes. The bill was a single page repealing the relevant sections of the tax code. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates — in 1989 the estate tax applied only to estates above roughly $600,000, so the direct benefit went almost entirely to families with substantial wealth. Wealthy individuals making large lifetime gifts would also have avoided the gift tax.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the estate tax entirely, so no estate of any size would owe federal estate tax after enactment [S3].
Repeals the gift tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax, removing taxes on large lifetime transfers and transfers designed to skip a generation [S3].
The repeal would apply to deaths and transfers occurring after the bill's enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes raise revenue from the wealthiest families; repealing them would shift that burden onto everyone else through higher other taxes, larger deficits, or reduced government services. Only estates large enough to owe the tax would gain directly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ordinary taxpayers who make up the difference

drawbacks.text: The bill contained no carve-out for family farms or small businesses, which supporters of estate-tax relief often cite; it repealed the tax across the board, concentrating its benefit on the largest estates [S3].
Repealing three revenue sources would reduce federal revenue collected from very wealthy families, leaving that money to be raised from other taxpayers or borrowed [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit goes exclusively to heirs of estates large enough to owe the tax, while the cost — lost federal revenue — is spread across everyone else. The common good-faith argument for estate-tax relief (protecting family farms and small businesses from forced sales) is not addressed here, because the bill offers a blanket repeal rather than targeted relief. As written, the transfer runs from the general taxpayer to the wealthiest families.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or voted on it, so the bill died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 4, 1989, by Rep. Philip M. Crane (R-IL) [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction, its only action in the Congress [S5].
No cosponsors signed on to the bill [S4].
The bill never advanced out of committee and received no vote before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained or lost money because the bill never moved; the estate tax remained in place, so no revenue shift occurred.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply died

for.name: Rep. Philip M. Crane
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan alignment can be measured.

industries.note: The estate tax in 1989 applied only to estates above roughly $600,000, so repeal would be a direct tax cut for the wealthiest families. Its cost — lost revenue — would be borne by taxpayers at large, so the industry's gain runs against the public's.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth advisory services
industries.note: Repeal would reduce demand for estate-tax planning, trusts, and life insurance bought to cover estate tax bills, while simplifying wealth transfer for clients. This is a general-knowledge inference, not something the bill text or record addresses.
